new-boston.lede: Water damage, mold remediation, fire and smoke cleanup, odor removal, and full reconstruction for New Boston homeowners and businesses — New Boston is the primary populated community within Huron Township in the southwestern corner of Wayne County.
local: New Boston is the primary populated community within Huron Township in the southwestern corner of Wayne County — a semi-rural area where residential development sits alongside active agricultural land, rural road corridors, and significant floodplain zones along the Huron River as it approaches Lake Erie. The housing stock is a mix of historic farmsteads and village-era construction dating back to the 19th century, rural residential development from the mid-20th century, and newer suburban-style builds that arrived as the I-275 corridor extended the commuter zone southward.

New Boston’s rural character means that many properties operate on well and septic rather than municipal water and sewer — a distinction that significantly changes the restoration profile for sewage backup and contamination events. Agricultural drainage patterns in Huron Township create water movement dynamics that differ from conventional suburban stormwater management, and the Huron River floodplain in this area is broader and less managed than it is further upstream, making flood events more extensive and longer-duration than comparable upstream scenarios.

new-boston.riskEyebrow: New Boston's Rural Character and Floodplain Position Create a Distinct Restoration Risk Profile
risk: The Huron River floodplain in the New Boston and Huron Township area is wider, flatter, and less constrained by urban infrastructure than the same river further upstream. When heavy precipitation drives significant runoff into the watershed, the resulting flood events in this area are slower to rise, slower to recede, and affect a larger footprint than comparable events in more channelized upstream areas. Properties in low-lying areas of Huron Township can experience extended periods of groundwater elevation that cause sustained basement moisture even after surface flooding recedes.

The presence of working farms and rural properties with well and septic systems in New Boston creates contamination scenarios that require a different assessment protocol than standard municipal sewer backup. When a septic system fails during a flooding event — a common scenario in rural Michigan communities — the resulting contamination classification and remediation requirements are more complex, more hazardous, and require more thorough documentation than a municipal sewer overflow.

northville.lede: Water damage, mold remediation, fire and smoke cleanup, odor removal, and complete reconstruction for Northville homeowners — historic Old Village properties near downtown and modern subdivisions throughout Northville Township.
local: Northville’s Old Village neighborhood near downtown contains some of the most historically significant residential architecture in the Metro Detroit area — Victorian, Colonial Revival, and Craftsman homes built between the 1870s and 1930s with original plaster, wide-plank hardwood, cast iron plumbing, and foundation systems predating modern waterproofing. These properties require a restoration approach calibrated to their age, materials, and architectural significance. Moisture behaves differently in original lath-and-plaster than it does in drywall. Cast iron drain lines fail differently than PVC. Block and stone foundations wick moisture in ways poured concrete doesn’t.

Beyond Old Village, Northville Township’s 1980s through 2010s subdivisions represent a fundamentally different housing profile — larger footprints, finished basements with premium materials, and the same aging builder-grade infrastructure issues that drive water damage calls across Oakland and Wayne Counties. Seven Mile Road, Six Mile Road, and the newer developments off Beck Road carry this newer construction. Restoring a finished basement flood in these areas is straightforward compared to the material complexity of an Old Village water event.

northville.riskEyebrow: Old Village Historic Homes and the Hidden Moisture Problem
risk: The historic homes throughout Northville’s Old Village were built with materials that absorb, hold, and distribute moisture differently than any modern construction. Plaster walls applied over wooden lath backing appear dry on the surface while the backing and framing behind them are saturated. Original wide-plank hardwood responds to saturation more slowly than engineered flooring — but warps differently and holds moisture far longer. Stone and block foundations in pre-war Northville construction wick moisture laterally through the masonry.

These dynamics mean an Old Village water event typically involves more affected area than visible damage suggests, a longer drying timeline than modern construction would require, and more careful scope assessment before demolition decisions are made. Like-kind-and-quality replacement for Northville’s original architectural elements — period millwork, original hardwood, plaster finish — requires contractor coordination beyond standard residential reconstruction.

The finished basements throughout Novi’s subdivisions are heavily outfitted — hardwood, built-in entertainment systems, home offices with custom cabinetry, and premium mechanicals are standard across mid-to-upper-range Novi housing. local: Plymouth City and Plymouth Township together form one of Wayne County’s most established and diverse communities. The historic homes near Old Village and downtown Plymouth — many dating to the early 1900s — carry original plaster walls, cast iron plumbing, and foundation systems that predate modern waterproofing standards. Restoring these properties after a water event means working carefully with materials that absorb moisture differently than drywall, hold it longer, and require extended drying timelines. The Rouge River’s North Branch runs through portions of the Plymouth area and creates specific flooding risk in lower-elevation properties during spring thaw.

Plymouth Township’s 1970s through 2000s subdivisions off Five Mile, Sheldon, and Ann Arbor Roads represent the majority of water damage call volume — finished basement flooding from sump failure, supply line breaks, and appliance failures in homes with varying levels of finish quality. The approach for a finished basement flood in a Township subdivision is faster and more straightforward than for a historic downtown Plymouth home, but the documentation standard and response urgency are the same.
